Spec revised and committed. **GATE 1 — spec approval.**

## Challenger verdict: NEEDS REWORK

It ran 66 tool calls and checked the spec's factual claims against source rather than trusting them. Its core judgment was right: **three of seven scenarios could not fail against the defect class they named.** A suite shipped as I first specified would have been the "conformance suite that cannot fail" the acceptance criteria exist to prevent.

## Folded in

**The four blockers, all legitimate:**

- **S4 could not fail assertion 6.** With no stop reason buffered, a driver that *wrongly* flushes `finish()` on the error arm emits no `Finish` either — nothing to flush. Correct and broken code both passed. Split into S4a/S4b; S4b buffers a stop reason first. SMA-531's design doc names "SMA-533's acceptance clause 6" as its reason for leaving Anthropic's dirty-cut arm unguarded — **this ticket was supposed to be the guard**, and my draft wasn't.
- **S5 had no synchronization edge.** The stop-reason chunk emits nothing observable for `openai/chat` or LiteLLM, so the test degenerated to sleep-and-hope — which `openai/tests/cancellation.rs:88-93` explicitly refuses to ship. Now S5b places an observable usage event before the gate, and the trait hands back a `GateHandle`.
- **Assertion 7 was satisfied by emitting no name at all.** "At most one" is the ticket's wording, but a translator that drops the name entirely passes it — exactly SMA-547's bug class. Tightened to **exactly one**, matching the fixture's declared name, plus a `NoNamedDelta` fake to prove it bites.
- **The stop-reason condition was declared suite-side but realized subject-side, with nothing reconciling them.** Now cross-checked via `encodes_stop_reason`.

**Also folded in:** hyper instead of raw TCP (request-body draining, `Expect: 100-continue` and abortable bodies are real, and their failures would present as provider bugs); a **fourth** `-core` doc site I missed (`ToolCallDelta` carries the positional wording on both the variant *and* the field); ordered violation classification, since assertions 1 and 2 overlap by construction; a pinned `DECLINED` set that fails on drift in either direction, so `Declined` can't become a quiet second escape hatch; the workspace-member enumeration, doc-coverage exposure, binary `.gitattributes` rule for Bedrock frames, per-scenario timeouts, new `[workspace.dependencies]` pins, and a coverage-delta table that re-sequences Bedrock first.

**One finding landed against my own §2.1.** `openai/backend/chat.rs:400-417` documents *against itself* that "a cross-provider conformance suite asserting 'at most one name-carrying delta per `call_id`' would fail here." My claim that assertion 7 needed no exception was too strong. The shape has no capture in the repo and is unobserved from any backend, so the provenance rule keeps it out of the fixture set and D4 survives — but it's now recorded as a known-uncovered shape with a follow-up ticket rather than glossed.

**S6's script was invented.** I specified "id resolving after the first fragment"; the committed capture's own header says the fragments "BOTH arrive after the id." I'd written a fixture from imagination in a spec whose §6 forbids exactly that. Now uses the committed shape.

## Rejected, with evidence

- **"Is SMA-550 actually merged?"** — it is. `git log origin/main --grep SMA-550` returns `0bf5e759`, and the merged source carries the canonicalization. The challenger inferred otherwise from `litellm/CHANGELOG.md` topping at 0.1.1, which just means release-plz's PR hasn't merged yet — normal.
- **"Gemini degenerates like Responses on S2"** — wrong. Gemini has two distinct terminal arms, `[DONE]` at `model.rs:156` and EOF at `:149`, so S2 exercises a path S1 doesn't. Only OpenAI Responses genuinely lacks the window; it declines S2/S4b/S5b.
- **`MockModel` ignores `_cancel`** — real, and a `Model` we ship that violates the clause we're tightening. But it isn't a provider, so it's a filed follow-up, not scope creep into this PR.
- **`ReasoningDelta` ordering, parallel tool calls, zero-arg tool calls** — declared out of scope. `Err` terminality was worth taking and is now folded into assertion 1.

## One thing for you

The core doc change **tightens a public trait's contract for third-party implementors** under a patch bump. It's doc-only and semver-compatible, but the spec now says the CHANGELOG and book should describe it as a contract clarification rather than a doc tweak. Say if you'd rather it stay understated.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/smaschek/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-20-sma-533-stream-conformance.md` (`3127c1e5`).

| Area | Files |

**Sequencing puts the risk first.** Task 3 is a Bedrock transport spike — SigV4 over local plain HTTP plus hand-built eventstream frames — with an explicit *stop and report* instruction. If the AWS SDK won't talk to `127.0.0.1` or the frames decode as `Unknown` and get silently dropped by the catch-all at `bedrock/src/stream.rs:244-246`, that must surface before five other subjects are written against the design. The plan names both failure signatures and what each means, because a dropped-frame failure reads as a translator bug and isn't one.

Tasks 4–6 build the checker with real test code first (11 checker tests, then 10 non-conformant fakes + a conforming one). Tasks 7–12 register the six subjects, Bedrock first since it has zero existing boundary coverage. Task 13 lands the wording; Task 14 runs the full gate list and files the four follow-ups.

## Stage 4 — implementation mode

**Recommendation: subagent-driven.** 14 tasks across a new crate, six providers, and four doc sites — far past the "1–2 tasks, single file" bar for inline execution. A fresh subagent per task with review between them also matches the repo's own lesson that a spec-conformant change can still carry regressions against `main`.

One caveat I'll enforce from the dispatch side: implementer subagents in this repo have a habit of backgrounding long `cargo` runs and ending their turn mid-task. Every dispatch will carry an explicit *work synchronously, foreground, don't end until terminal status* instruction, plus the no-branch-moving-git guard since this is a shared checkout.

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are: BLOCKED status you cannot resolve, ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: STOP. Append `Task <N>: BLOCKED — <reason>` and report to
  your human partner with the finding, the plan text it collides with, and
  the fix history. Parking a structural failure lets every dependent task
  build on it and hands the final review a problem it cannot fix either.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).

## Common Rationalizations

|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |

| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |

Good catch on concern 1 — that is exactly the vacuous-pass hazard this suite exists to prevent, and you found it in your own code. One follow-up before I send this to review.

**Add a regression test for the deferred-error flush.** Your report says the defer-by-one-poll in `script_frames` is load-bearing and that no committed test covers it — a client can receive **zero body bytes** while `abort_ending_surfaces_as_an_error` still passes. Write a test that asserts the abort path delivers **both** halves of the contract:
1. the client observes the chunks that were sent before the abort, and
2. the read still terminates as an error, not a clean EOF.

Assert on the actual bytes received, so the test fails if the body arrives empty. `reqwest`'s `bytes_stream()` lets you accumulate what arrived before the error surfaces. Name it for what it protects — something like `abort_delivers_buffered_chunks_before_erroring`.

Then confirm it is a real test by mutating the production code the way a future simplification would: remove the defer-by-one-poll so the error escapes before the flush, run the new test, and record that it FAILS. Restore the defer and record that it passes. Put that mutation evidence in your report — a test that cannot fail is worse than no test here.

Also add a short `//` comment at the defer site saying why it exists and pointing at the test name, so the next reader does not "simplify" it.

- Your `gate_after` clarification is right and I am propagating it — later tasks will be told it is a **count**, not an index.
- Concern 3 (test 3's 200 ms window) I am accepting as-is; it is inherent to the given test and the gate dependency is already proven by your mutation check.

Re-run the covering tests, append a fix report to the same report file with the command and output plus the mutation evidence, and reply with the same short status contract.

Task review is back. Approved on quality, with one Important finding to fix. Your work is solid — this is about the *evidence*, not the code.

**Finding — the committed test does not prove the half of assumption 1 you claim it proves.**

Your report says assumption 1 is PROVEN and cites a captured raw socket showing a real `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` signature. That probe was not committed. What *is* committed proves only the narrower claim: that `BedrockModel::invoke` round-trips over plain HTTP to `127.0.0.1`. It says nothing about the signature, because — as your own doc comment at `eventstream.rs:174` concedes — `PacedServer` ignores the `Authorization` header entirely. A request with a broken or entirely missing `Authorization` header would pass the committed test exactly as well as a correctly signed one.

That gap matters more here than it normally would. This task's *entire purpose* is to be reproducible proof for five dependent tasks. A spike whose strongest claim rests on scaffolding that no longer exists is a spike that has to be re-run by hand the next time anyone doubts it. The reviewer independently checked that SigV4 signing is an unconditional step in the generated client's pipeline, so the assumption is very likely true — but "very likely true" is what this task existed to replace.

**Fix: make the proof reproducible.** Have `PacedServer` capture the request headers it received and expose them, then assert in the test that `Authorization` is present and starts with `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256`. You already drain the request body, so the head is in hand — this should be small. Keep the accessor narrow; a `received_headers()` or a captured-`Authorization` accessor is enough, and do not turn `PacedServer` into a general request-recording mock.

**Prove the assertion can fail**, the same way you did for the frame headers: make the client send no valid signature (or assert against a deliberately wrong prefix) and confirm the new assertion fails. Record it.

**Then correct the report.** Restate the assumption-1 verdict in terms of what the committed tests actually re-verify. If after this fix the committed suite proves both the plain-HTTP dispatch and the signature prefix, say exactly that. The next person to read `task-3-report.md` will treat it as settled fact, so it needs to be accurate about its own basis.

**No action needed on these — recorded, not for this round:**
- Your `Finish` assertion checks only the variant, not `reason == FinishReason::Stop`. That is verbatim from the brief, so it is my defect rather than yours; Task 7 will pin the reason.
- The model-id inconsistency you self-flagged (`…-20240620-v1:0` vs the crate's `…-20241022-v2:0`) is harmless — both resolve to `ModelFamily::Anthropic`.
- I verified all six workspace dependency pins already exist in the root manifest, so nothing was missing there.

Re-run the covering tests, append a fix report to the same report file with the command, output, and the mutation result, and reply with the same short status contract.

The Bedrock spike — the one task that could have forced a redesign — **passed on both assumptions**, and the plan is corrected where the spike falsified it.

**Progress: 2 of 14 complete, Task 3 in fix round 1.**

| Task | State |
|---|---|
| 1 — crate scaffold, types, registration | ✅ clean first pass |
| 2 — paced hyper server | ✅ clean after 1 fix round |
| 3 — Bedrock spike | both assumptions proven; fixing the *evidence* |

**What the spike settled.** The AWS SDK does sign SigV4 and talk plain HTTP to `127.0.0.1` via `SdkConfig::endpoint_url`, and hand-built eventstream frames decode into real translator output. Both were mutation-checked in *both* directions — corrupting `:event-type` reproduces the silent-drop signature the plan warned about (`got []`, no error), and forcing HTTPS reproduces the transport failure. So the `StaticReplayClient` fallback in spec §11 is not needed, and no Bedrock scenario has to be declined for transport reasons.

**Three plan corrections** came out of it, now committed in `cb8912e4`: the smithy crates had to move from `[dev-dependencies]` to `[dependencies]` (my brief was wrong — `frame` is a lib item called from an integration test, and dev-deps aren't linkable there); the builder entry is `BedrockModel::converse(...)`, not `builder(...)`; and `build_bedrock_model_against` is `#[cfg(test)]`, so Task 7 must copy it rather than import it. The spike also pinned down retry behaviour that Tasks 7–12 need: a mid-body abort after a 200 is **not** retried, which is what makes S4a/S4b viable for Bedrock at all.

**The fix in flight is about proof, not code.** The reviewer caught that the report's strongest claim — a captured raw socket showing `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` — rested on scaffolding that was deleted before commit. The committed test only proves plain-HTTP dispatch, because `PacedServer` ignores the `Authorization` header, so an unsigned request would pass it identically. For a task whose entire purpose is to be durable proof for five dependent tasks, "very likely true" is exactly what it existed to replace. It's now capturing the header and asserting the prefix.

Continuing through Tasks 4–14. Next natural checkpoint is Task 7, the first real provider registration, where the suite starts returning verdicts about production code rather than about itself.

This is SMA-533 in the Paigasus Helikon Rust SDK: a cross-provider conformance suite asserting the `Model::invoke` stream event-ordering contract against six provider translators at the HTTP boundary. You are building the last piece of infrastructure. Tasks 7–12 each register one provider and call `assert_conforms`; nothing after this task touches the harness.

## Interfaces you consume (all committed)

- `pub fn classify(events: &[Result<ModelEvent, ModelError>], scenario: Scenario, cancelled: bool) -> Option<Violation>` — re-exported at the crate root from a private `check` module.

## Three things that decide whether this harness is worth having

**1. The floors run before the assertions.** A stream that emits nothing satisfies "ends with `Finish`" trivially, and a miswired adapter serving the wrong fixture would pass every assertion by producing nothing at all. The brief lists the per-scenario floors; they are the reason a vacuous pass fails loudly instead of reading as success.

**2. The decline set is pinned in both directions.** `Outcome::Declined` is otherwise a second escape hatch with none of the rigor the process demands — a future engineer facing a red assertion could turn it into `Declined("wire shape cannot occur")` in one line and keep CI green. So the suite must fail on an **unexpected** decline *and* on an **expected decline that stopped happening**. The second direction matters as much as the first: a decline that silently starts passing means the table is now lying about the provider.

**3. A cancellation scenario must prove it actually observed truncation.** This one is not in the brief — I am adding it from a Task 2 review finding. Dropping a `GateHandle` releases the body, so if a subject returns `Outcome::Served { gate: None, .. }` for a cancel scenario, or the gate is dropped early, the scenario silently degrades into an ungated one that passes vacuously. Per scenario: call `stream`; on `Declined` record and continue; on `Served` first cross-check `subject.encodes_stop_reason(scenario)` against `scenario.expects_stop_reason()` and fail with `StopReasonDeclarationMismatch` if they disagree; then drain (with the gate/cancel dance for the two cancel scenarios); then floors; then `classify`. Good work, and thank you for flagging all six rather than quietly picking. Decisions below.

**Concern 4 — implement it. This is my omission, and now is the only cheap moment to fix it.**

The design spec §7.1 requires: "S1 and S7 must yield exactly one `Finish`, **with the `FinishReason` the fixture declares**." My brief dropped that clause and gave `StreamUnderTest` no way to express it. Tasks 7–12 have not been written yet, so adding a trait method costs nothing now and would cost six subject rewrites later.

Add to `StreamUnderTest`:

```rust
/// The `FinishReason` this subject's fixture for `scenario` declares, or
/// `None` for scenarios that must not produce a `Finish` at all.
fn fixture_finish_reason(&self, scenario: Scenario) -> Option<FinishReason>;
```

Enforce it in the floors for `CleanStop` and `ToolCallCleanStop`: the single `Finish` must carry exactly that reason. Fail with a message naming the subject, the scenario, the expected reason and the observed one. Keep it in the floor rather than in `classify` — `classify` has no fixture knowledge and its signature is fixed.

This also closes a Minor from Task 3's review: that spike's `Finish` assertion checked only the variant, never `reason == Stop`. This is where that gets pinned.

**Concern 1 — your ordering is right; the brief was wrong.** Releasing the gate before firing the token races the terminator against the token and would report `FinishOnCancel` against a correct provider. Holding the gate across cancellation and using `GateHandle::release`'s "was the server still parked" as the truncation proof is a better design than what I specified, and it satisfies the truncation requirement I gave you more directly. Keep it. Make sure the reasoning is a comment at the site, not only in your report — the next reader will otherwise "fix" it back.

**Concern 2 — keep it, but make the constant self-documenting.** Your point about Anthropic emitting `Usage` at `message_start` is a real falsification of my §6.1 "gate on an observable event" design: it would silently degrade S5b into S5a for that subject. Quiescence is the right call. But 400 ms is a timing constant, so name it, comment *why* quiescence rather than a named edge, and state what happens on a slow machine. If a slow machine makes it fire late rather than early, say so — late is safe, early is what would corrupt the scenario.

**Concerns 3 and 6 — agreed, no change.** Leaving excess to `classify` so the SMA-550 shape reports `ToolNameNotExactlyOnce` rather than `InsufficientEvidence` is exactly right; a floor that swallowed it would hide the finding this suite exists to surface. And adding the nine-test harness module rather than shipping `assert_conforms` untested was the correct instinct — `Fake::run` calling `classify` directly does leave the floors uncovered.

**5 of 14 complete.** Task 6 — the last piece of infrastructure — is in a fix round.

Task 6's implementer did the most valuable thing any of them has done so far: it **refused two of my instructions and was right both times.**

**It rejected my cancel ordering.** My brief said release the gate, then fire the token. That races the stream terminator against the cancellation — so a *correct* provider that emits `Finish` from the released body before the token lands would be reported as `FinishOnCancel`. The suite would have manufactured violations against conforming code. It holds the gate across cancellation instead, and uses "was the server still parked when released" as positive proof of truncation — which satisfies the requirement I'd added from Task 2's review more directly than my own design did.

**It falsified my §6.1 gate design.** The spec says place an observable event after the stop reason and cancel on seeing it. But Anthropic emits `Usage` at `message_start` — so "cancel on first `Usage`" would fire before the stop reason was ever buffered, silently degrading S5b into S5a for that subject. That's a design flaw I wrote into the approved spec and the challenger didn't catch. It switched to stream quiescence; I've asked for the timing constant to be named and justified, and flagged it for the reviewer rather than waving it through.

**One decision was mine to make.** Spec §7.1 requires that S1 and S7 assert the *specific* `FinishReason` the fixture declares — and my brief dropped the clause entirely, leaving `StreamUnderTest` with no way to express it. Review is back: **Approved on quality**, and it verified your load-bearing claims against the real code rather than taking them on report. Specifically it confirmed `server_was_parked` is genuine evidence — `feed` is a detached task whose gate receiver outlives the client disconnect, so `release()` still returns `true` after cancellation tears down the connection, and it returns `false` only in the degenerate `gate_after > chunks.len()` case. Both deviations stand.

Three things to fix.

**1. Important — `CancelAfterStopReason` is the one degradation path with no detector.**

Every other way a cancel scenario can silently degrade has an explicit check: `gate: None`, `fired`, `server_was_parked`. S5b→S5a has none. Its floor is only "≥ 1 `TokenDelta`", and the `encodes_stop_reason` cross-check compares a subject-declared value against `scenario.expects_stop_reason()` — which the subject skeleton implements *as* `scenario.expects_stop_reason()`, so it can never fail for a subject following the template.

The failure: a Task 8/9/11 author sets `gate_after` one chunk too early, withholding both the stop-reason chunk and the usage chunk after it. The harness sees only `TokenDelta`s, quiesces, cancels, gets `fired` + `server_was_parked` + a passing floor, and reports green — while the scenario actually ran S5a and the S5b assertion (a driver wrongly flushing a *buffered* stop reason on cancel) was never exercised. That is the vacuous-pass class the rest of this task exists to close.

Fix: require ≥ 1 `Usage` in the drained events for `CancelAfterStopReason`. That discriminates a misplaced gate for openai/chat, litellm and gemini at zero cost, and it matches the fixture rule the brief already states ("the script must place a usage chunk after it and gate on that").

It is **vacuous for anthropic** — `message_start` emits `Usage`, so the floor passes trivially there. Say so in the floor comment, and note that anthropic's guarantee has to come from its fixture's provenance comment instead. Record that narrowing at the site the way you recorded the other two, so it is visible rather than implied.

**2. Minor — the `GATE_QUIESCENCE` doc's stated consequence is wrong for the case it omits** (`src/lib.rs:234-240`). The doc argues early firing needs two consecutive pre-gate chunks 400 ms apart. But the timer re-arms per event, and the *first* arming covers the window between `drain` being polled and the first event, when nothing has been consumed. If that window elapsed, the token fires with zero events and the run fails the "no TokenDelta" floor — a spurious failure, which contradicts the sentence claiming the consequence is "a weaker test rather than a spurious failure". The mechanism is fine (the real window is sub-millisecond); the sentence is wrong. Fix it — six later tasks will read that doc while debugging an intermittent cancel failure, and as written it points them away from the timing.

**3. Minor — `fixture_finish_reason` is required for `TruncatedAfterStopReason` but never checked** (trait doc `src/lib.rs:195-204` vs the floor gate at `src/lib.rs:541`). A subject can declare anything there and get no signal, while assertion 3 forces a `Finish` whose reason is just as forgeable as `CleanStop`'s. Add `TruncatedAfterStopReason` to that `matches!`. - **Modify:** `tests/provider-stream-conformance/tests/conformance.rs` — add a `mod openai_chat { … }` block alongside the existing `mod bedrock { … }`

Read `tests/provider-stream-conformance/tests/conformance.rs` first. Task 7

helper functions, an exhaustive `script(scenario)` match, an exhaustive
`fixture_finish_reason` match, and a **measured** `encodes_stop_reason`. Follow it.

- `assert_conforms(&subject).await`
- `StreamUnderTest` — five methods: `name`, `encodes_stop_reason`, `fixture_tool_name`, `fixture_finish_reason`, `stream`

- `PacedServer::start(script).await`, `.base_url()`, `.take_gate()`
- `Script { content_type, chunks, gate_after, ending }`, `Ending::{Clean, Abort}`

**`gate_after` is a COUNT, not an index.** `Some(n)` pauses after `n` chunks.

Content type is `text/event-stream`. Each chunk is one SSE frame:
`b"data: {json}\n\n"`. The builder entry point is
`OpenAiModel::chat("gpt-4o-mini").base_url(server.base_url()).build()`.

Task 7 established that this must **measure the bytes you are about to serve**, not
restate `scenario.expects_stop_reason()`. The latter makes the harness's
cross-check dead code, and it is the only detector for `ErrorAfterStopReason`

**The obvious marker is wrong.** OpenAI emits `"finish_reason":null` on ordinary

the opening quote of a non-null value, e.g. `"finish_reason":"`. Pin this with a
guard test in the shape of bedrock's `scan_finds_only_the_stop_event`: assert the

| --- | --- |
| `CleanStop` | content deltas → chunk with `finish_reason` → **chunk carrying `usage`** → `[DONE]` → clean end |
| `TruncatedAfterStopReason` | content deltas → chunk with `finish_reason` → body ends cleanly, no `usage`, no `[DONE]` |

| `ErrorAfterStopReason` | content deltas → chunk with `finish_reason` → `Ending::Abort` |
| `CancelMidGeneration` | content deltas → gate → harness cancels |
| `CancelAfterStopReason` | content deltas → `finish_reason` chunk → **`usage` chunk** → gate → harness cancels |

# Task 10: Register `anthropic` in the stream conformance suite

From `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-20-sma-533-stream-conformance.md`, section
"Tasks 7 to 12: Register the six subjects", specialised for the Anthropic Messages
provider.

`anthropic` serves **eight scenarios** and declines one. It is the provider whose
truncation defect (SMA-531, PR #200) is half the reason this suite exists.

## Files

- **Modify:** `tests/provider-stream-conformance/tests/conformance.rs` — add `mod anthropic { … }`
- **Modify:** `tests/provider-stream-conformance/Cargo.toml` — add `paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic` as a dev-dep

## Copy the established shape

Read `tests/provider-stream-conformance/tests/conformance.rs` first. `mod openai_chat`
and `mod litellm` are the reviewed patterns. Match their structure: scoped module,
chunk-builder helpers each citing a source fixture, an exhaustive `script(scenario)`
match, an exhaustive `fixture_finish_reason` match, a **measured** `encodes_stop_reason`,
and a marker guard test. Use unprefixed helper names inside your module.

**`gate_after` is a COUNT, not an index** — `Some(n)` pauses after `n` chunks. Two
earlier subjects shipped a gate comment that miscounted; check yours against your own
script rather than copying prose.

## Wire format

Content type `text/event-stream`. Anthropic frames carry an explicit event name:

```
event: content_block_delta\ndata: {json}\n\n
```

Builder: `AnthropicModel::messages("claude-3-5-sonnet-latest").base_url(server.base_url()).build()`
— confirmed present at `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/src/model.rs:29`.

## What is different about this provider — read before scripting

**1. `message_delta` carries the stop reason AND usage in the same event.** That is
why this subject can serve `CancelAfterStopReason` at all: it has an observable event
at the moment the stop reason is buffered.

**2. `message_start` also emits a `Usage`.** This makes the harness's
`CancelAfterStopReason` floor — "at least one `Usage` observed" — **vacuous for this
subject**: it is satisfied by `message_start` alone, whether or not the gate sits in
the right place. The harness records this at the floor site. Your obligation is to
make the guarantee visible where it can be checked: **the fixture's provenance
comment must show the gate sitting after `message_delta`**, and say so explicitly.
That comment is the only guard for this scenario on this subject.

**3. The stop reason appears as `"stop_reason":null` in `message_start`.** So a naive
scan for `stop_reason` matches an event carrying no stop reason at all. Your
`encodes_stop_reason` marker must distinguish a *populated* value — `"stop_reason":"`.
Pin it with a guard test asserting the marker is absent from a `message_start` frame.

This measured check is the only detector for `ErrorAfterStopReason` degrading into
`ErrorMidGeneration` — their observable events are byte-identical.

## Scenarios

`DECLINED` in `src/declines.rs` has exactly **one** row for `anthropic`:
`FragmentedToolName`, reason "name arrives whole in content_block_start". Read the
exact string from that file rather than retyping it — the harness fails if the
observed decline set differs from the pinned one in either direction, including a
reworded reason.

| Scenario | Script |
| --- | --- |
| `CleanStop` | `message_start` → `content_block_start` → deltas → `content_block_stop` → `message_delta` (stop reason + usage) → `message_stop` → clean end |
| `TruncatedAfterStopReason` | … → `message_delta` → body ends cleanly, **no `message_stop`** |
| `TruncatedMidGeneration` | `message_start` → `content_block_start` → deltas → body ends cleanly |
| `ErrorMidGeneration` | deltas → `Ending::Abort`, no `message_delta` |
| `ErrorAfterStopReason` | … → `message_delta` → `Ending::Abort` |
| `CancelMidGeneration` | deltas → gate → harness cancels |
| `CancelAfterStopReason` | … → `message_delta` → gate → harness cancels |
| `FragmentedToolName` | **Declined** |
| `ToolCallCleanStop` | `content_block_start` with `tool_use` → `input_json_delta`s → `content_block_stop` → `message_delta` (`tool_use` stop reason) → `message_stop` |

`TruncatedAfterStopReason` is the **exact SMA-531 shape**: a stream truncated between
`message_delta` and `message_stop`. Before the fix, that emitted `Usage` and no
`Finish` at all. It must now produce exactly one `Finish`.

## Provenance — this crate's fixtures map almost one-to-one onto the scenarios

Fixtures are transcribed from captured or already-committed traffic, never invented
from vendor docs. `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/tests/fixtures/`:

- `text_only.txt` — the baseline text stream
- `eof_after_message_delta.txt` — **`TruncatedAfterStopReason`**, the SMA-531 shape
- `eof_mid_content_block.txt` — **`TruncatedMidGeneration`**
- `error_after_message_delta.txt` — **`ErrorAfterStopReason`**
- `stream_error.txt` — a mid-stream error frame
- `body_cut_inside_message_stop.txt`
- `tool_use_then_continuation.txt`, `parallel_tool_use.txt` — tool shapes
- `thinking_then_text.txt`

Cite the specific file each shape came from. If a shape cannot be grounded that way,
**stop and report** rather than inventing one.

Note `.gitattributes` already pins `tests/provider-stream-conformance/fixtures/**/*.txt`
to `text eol=lf`; the anthropic crate's own fixtures are likewise LF-pinned because
the streaming tests split on literal `\n`.

## Steps

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the module**

- [ ] **Step 2: Run it — expect failure first**

```bash
cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-provider-stream-conformance --test conformance anthropic
```

Read every failure before changing anything.

- [ ] **Step 3: Triage each failure**

- A fixture or registration bug → fix it here.
- A small, obvious provider defect → fix it, note it in the commit body.
- A defect needing a design decision → **stop and surface it.** No `#[ignore]`, no new
  `DECLINED` row without human sign-off.

- [ ] **Step 4: Prove the green is not vacuous**

Two mutations, both recorded:

1. Remove the populated stop reason from `ErrorAfterStopReason`'s script; it must fail
   with `StopReasonDeclarationMismatch`.
2. **Reproduce SMA-531**: in `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/src/model.rs`,
   disable the end-of-stream `finish()` flush so a truncated stream emits no `Finish`.
   `TruncatedAfterStopReason` must fail with `MissingFinish`. **Revert fully** and
   confirm with `git diff --stat -- crates/` before committing — a reviewer will check.

- [ ] **Step 5: Run the whole suite, then commit**

```bash
cargo fmt --all
cargo clippy -p paigasus-helikon-provider-stream-conformance --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-provider-stream-conformance
```

```bash
git commit -m "test(providers): SMA-533 register anthropic in the stream conformance suite"
```

From `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-20-sma-533-stream-conformance.md`, section
"Tasks 7 to 12: Register the six subjects", specialised for the OpenAI Responses
backend. **This is the last subject.**

`openai/responses` serves **five scenarios** and declines **four** — more than any
other subject, and for one structural reason.

## Files

- **Modify:** `tests/provider-stream-conformance/tests/conformance.rs` — add `mod openai_responses { … }`
- The `paigasus-helikon-providers-openai` dev-dep already exists from Task 8

## Copy the established shape

`mod openai_chat`, `mod litellm`, `mod anthropic` and `mod gemini` are all reviewed.
Match their structure: scoped module, chunk-builder helpers each citing a source, an
exhaustive `script(scenario)` match, an exhaustive `fixture_finish_reason` match, a
**measured** `encodes_stop_reason`, and a marker guard test. Unprefixed helper names
inside the module.

**`gate_after` is a COUNT, not an index.** Check any gate comment against your own
script — two subjects shipped one that miscounted.

Builder: `OpenAiModel::responses("gpt-4o-mini").base_url(server.base_url()).build()`
(`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-openai/src/model.rs:34`). Content type
`text/event-stream`. Responses frames are typed SSE events —
`event: response.output_text.delta\ndata: {json}\n\n`.

## Why this subject declines four scenarios

`terminal_events` (`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-openai/src/backend/responses.rs:454-489`)
builds **`Usage` and `Finish` together from a single upstream event**. There is no
window in which a stop reason has been observed but `Finish` has not yet been
emitted. The driver at `responses.rs:70` is `None => return` with **no flush at all**
— this backend has no `finish()` method.

That makes three scenarios unreachable, plus the tool-name one:

| Scenario | Status |
| --- | --- |
| `CleanStop` | ✅ served |
| `TruncatedAfterStopReason` | ❌ declined — "stop reason and Finish are the same event" |
| `TruncatedMidGeneration` | ✅ served |
| `ErrorMidGeneration` | ✅ served |
| `ErrorAfterStopReason` | ❌ declined — "stop reason and Finish are the same event" |
| `CancelMidGeneration` | ✅ served |
| `CancelAfterStopReason` | ❌ declined — "stop reason and Finish are the same event" |
| `FragmentedToolName` | ❌ declined — "name arrives whole in output_item.added" |
| `ToolCallCleanStop` | ✅ served |

`DECLINED` in `src/declines.rs` has exactly **four** rows for `openai/responses`.
**Read the exact strings from that file** — three of them share identical wording,
and the harness fails if the observed decline set differs from the pinned one in
either direction, including a reworded reason.

input.title: openai/responses reports Finish{ToolCalls} for a function call that streams no argument deltas
input.description:
Surfaced by the SMA-533 conformance suite while fixing the missing `FinishReason::ToolCalls` mapping on the Responses backend. Pre-existing root cause; the SMA-533 fix changed which way it fails.

## The defect

`ResponsesTranslator` populates `item_to_call` from `response.output_item.added` alone (`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-openai/src/backend/responses.rs:331-345`), but only emits a `ToolCallDelta` when an argument delta arrives.

So a function call that streams **zero** `response.function_call_arguments.delta` frames — a no-argument tool, if the API elides them — now yields `Finish { reason: ToolCalls }` with **no `ToolCallDelta` at all**, telling an agent loop there are calls to run when none were emitted.

Before the SMA-533 fix this case yielded `Finish { reason: Stop }`: also wrong, but it failed safe.

## Root cause

The translator ignores `response.output_item.done`, which carries the complete `arguments` string. A call whose arguments never streamed incrementally is therefore invisible to the delta path even though the terminal item describes it fully.

## Reachability

Unconfirmed. The live capture taken 2026-08-20 (`gpt-4o-mini`, one `get_weather` tool with a required `city` argument) streamed five argument deltas, so this shape was not observed. A zero-argument tool is the obvious candidate and was not tested.

## Acceptance criteria

* Determine whether a zero-argument tool call streams any `function_call_arguments.delta` frames, by capture rather than by reading docs.
* If reachable, emit the tool call from `output_item.done` so the `ToolCallDelta` and the `Finish{ToolCalls}` agree.
* A test drives the zero-delta sequence and asserts the two agree, verified to fail against the current translator.

input.title: paigasus-helikon-evals MockModel ignores its cancellation token
input.description:
Found while writing the SMA-533 cross-provider stream conformance suite. Not a provider, so out of that suite's scope, but it is a `Model` this workspace ships that violates a contract the workspace documents.

## The defect

`crates/paigasus-helikon-evals/src/mock.rs:48-62` ignores its `_cancel` argument entirely.

`paigasus_helikon_core::Model::invoke` requires:

> Implementations that cannot honor cancellation MUST still terminate the stream when the `CancellationToken` fires (drop the underlying connection and end the stream without emitting `Finish`).

`MockModel` would therefore fail the conformance suite's assertion 5 (cancellation emits no `Finish`) if it were registered as a subject.

## Why it matters

`MockModel` is what consumers reach for when testing their own agent loops. A mock that ignores cancellation lets a consumer's cancellation handling look correct under test and fail against a real provider — the mock is the one place this is least likely to be noticed.

## Note

`RetryingModel` (`crates/paigasus-helikon-runtime-tokio/src/retry.rs:169-231`) is conformant only incidentally: it retries strictly before the first item. Worth pinning that with a test in the same change.

## Acceptance criteria

* `MockModel` terminates its stream when the token fires, without emitting `Finish`.
* A test asserts it, verified to fail against the current implementation.

input.title: Unify the stream translator finish() return shape across the six providers
input.description:
Deferred out of SMA-533. That ticket asked to "settle the `finish()` return shape"; the conformance suite it added asserts at the `Model::invoke` boundary and never observes `finish()`, so unifying it served no assertion there and would have mixed a five-crate signature refactor into a test-adding change.

## The divergence — four shapes, not the three the original ticket listed

| Subject | `consume` returns | `finish()` returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openai/backend/chat` | `Vec<ModelEvent>` | `Vec<ModelEvent>` |
| `openai/backend/responses` | `Result<Vec<ModelEvent>, ModelError>` | *(absent)* |
| `anthropic` | `Result<Vec<Result<ModelEvent, ModelError>>, ModelError>` | `Option<Result<ModelEvent, ModelError>>` |
| `bedrock` | `Vec<Result<ModelEvent, ModelError>>` | `Option<Result<ModelEvent, ModelError>>` |
| `gemini` | `Vec<Result<ModelEvent, ModelError>>` | `Vec<Result<ModelEvent, ModelError>>` |
| `litellm` | `Vec<ModelEvent>` | `Vec<ModelEvent>` |

`openai/backend/responses` has **no `finish()` at all** — its `terminal_events` builds `Usage` and `Finish` together from one upstream event, and its driver is a bare `None => return` with no flush.

## Why it is safer to do now

The SMA-533 suite exercises all six drivers end to end at the HTTP boundary, including truncation, cancellation and mid-stream error paths. A refactor of the flush signatures is now guarded by tests that did not exist when the divergence was flagged.

## Note

Any candidate design has to account for `responses` genuinely not needing a flush, rather than adding an empty one for symmetry.

## Acceptance criteria

* One shape across all six, or a documented rationale at each site that keeps a different one.
* The conformance suite stays green throughout, and no provider's observable event sequence changes.

input.title: gemini live tests default to gemini-2.5-flash, which 404s for new API users
input.description:
Found while capturing a live Gemini tool-call stream for the SMA-533 conformance suite on 2026-08-20.

## The defect

`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini/tests/live.rs:17` defaults `GEMINI_MODEL_ID` to `gemini-2.5-flash`. Against a Developer API key today that returns:

```
404 NOT_FOUND: This model models/gemini-2.5-flash is no longer available to new users.
Please update your code to use models/gemini-3.6-flash for the latest features and improvements.
```

`gemini-3.6-flash` works and was used for the capture.

## Why it is easy to miss

The live tests are env-gated and loud-skip without a credential, so CI never exercises this path. Anyone running them fresh gets a 404 that looks like a provider or auth problem rather than a stale default.

## Scope

Small. Bump the default and check whether the same model id appears elsewhere — the docs, the book, or other crates' examples.

## Acceptance criteria

* The default model id resolves for a new API key.
* Any other occurrence of the retired id in the repo is updated or removed.

input.title: openai/chat emits two name-carrying deltas for one call_id given the same id under different indexes
input.description:
The translator documents this against itself at `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-openai/src/backend/chat.rs:400-417`, and closes with: *"A cross-provider conformance suite asserting 'at most one name-carrying delta per `call_id`' would fail here and pass for litellm; closing it needs its own ticket."* This is that ticket.

## The defect

Given two tool-call deltas carrying **different `index` values but the same `id`**, this translator keeps two index-keyed entries and emits a name for each — two name-carrying `ToolCallDelta`s for one `call_id`.

`providers-litellm` does not have this gap: SMA-550 canonicalized its correlation state onto the resolved `call_id`, so one `call_id` owns exactly one state entry. The two translators are deliberately aligned elsewhere, and this is the one place they diverge — in the direction where `openai/chat` is the weaker one.

## Why the SMA-533 suite does not catch it

The shape is malformed (an `id` identifies a call, so two indexes sharing one is contradictory) and is unobserved from any backend. It has **no capture anywhere in this repo**, so under that suite's provenance rule — fixtures are transcribed from captured traffic, never invented — it is not in the fixture set. Assertion 7 is therefore green for `openai/chat` without an `#[ignore]`, and the gap is real but unexercised.

## Options

* Canonicalize on the resolved `call_id` the way SMA-550 did for litellm, restoring alignment.
* Or add a `call_id`-level dedup to `flush_buffered_names`, which currently has none.

## Acceptance criteria

* A test drives two deltas with different `index` and the same `id`, asserting at most one name-carrying `ToolCallDelta` per `call_id`.
* The test is verified to FAIL against the current translator.
* The behavioural alignment with `providers-litellm` is restored, or the remaining divergence is documented in a code comment at both sites.

input.title: Extend the stream conformance suite to reasoning deltas, parallel tool calls and post-error events
input.description:
Coverage gaps recorded during SMA-533, which deliberately scoped itself to the seven assertions in its own design doc.

## Not covered by the suite today

**1. `ReasoningDelta` ordering.** No scenario emits one. Anthropic (extended thinking), OpenAI (o-series/gpt-5) and Gemini all produce them, and their interleaving with `TokenDelta` is unasserted across every provider.

**2. Parallel tool calls.** Every tool scenario drives a single call. `ModelCapabilities` has a parallel-tool-call flag and `anthropic` ships a `parallel_tool_use.txt` fixture, so the shape is real and capturable. Assertion 7 is per-`call_id`, so multiple concurrent calls are exactly where a correlation bug would show.

**3. Events emitted after an `Err`.** `classify` guards what follows `Finish` but nothing constrains what follows an `Err`. A translator that keeps draining after an upstream error is unclassified by all five rules. Plausible from a broken translator; not in the design's assertion list.

**4. Zero-argument tool calls.** Related to the Responses-backend defect filed separately — no scenario drives a tool call that streams no argument deltas.

## Note on how to add these

The suite's provenance rule is load-bearing: fixtures are transcribed from captured or already-committed traffic, never invented from vendor documentation. Two shapes in SMA-533 had to be captured live rather than derived, and one derived shape was reverted in review for exactly this reason. Any new scenario needs a capture behind it.

## Acceptance criteria

* Each new assertion has a non-conformant fake proving it can fail, matching the existing `Fake` pattern.
* Each new scenario declares its declines in the pinned `DECLINED` table where a provider cannot express the shape.
* Every new fixture cites captured traffic.

input.content:
Adds a cross-provider conformance suite that asserts the `Model::invoke` stream event-ordering contract against all six provider translators at the HTTP boundary, and lands the `-core` contract wording that suite enforces — so prose and test cannot drift.

## Why this is a `fix`, not a `test`

The suite found a real, previously-unknown defect in shipped code. `openai/responses` reported `Finish { reason: Stop }` on a tool-call turn where all five sibling providers report `ToolCalls` — `terminal_events` had no `ToolCalls` arm at all. It is consumer-visible only (the agent loop dispatches on the presence of `Item::ToolCall` and discards `finish_reason`), but it is exactly the cross-provider inconsistency this work set out to surface.

The pre-fix failure, verbatim:

```
openai/responses / ToolCallCleanStop — FinishReasonMismatch { expected: ToolCalls, observed: Stop }
```

Fixed in one guarded match arm, with every other arm provably unchanged, covered by four unit tests plus a capture-backed wire test.

## What it asserts

Seven properties, over nine wire scenarios, against six subjects:

1. `Finish` is terminal — nothing follows it, at most one is emitted
2. `Usage` precedes `Finish` when present
3. EOF after an observed stop reason emits `Finish`
4. No stop reason observed ⇒ no `Finish` — truncation is never reported as a clean stop
5. Cancellation emits no `Finish`
6. A mid-stream error emits no `Finish`
7. **Exactly** one `ToolCallDelta` per `call_id` carries `Some(name)` — deliberately tightened from the ticket's "at most one", which a translator that drops the name entirely would satisfy

## Proof that it can fail

A conformance suite that cannot fail is the failure mode that let the original defect ship, so this is built in rather than checked once:

- **Both motivating defects were reproduced in shipped code and caught.** Disabling Anthropic's end-of-stream `finish()` flush yields `MissingFinish` with the exact pre-fix sequence `Usage, TokenDelta, TokenDelta, Usage`. Reproducing the OpenAI Chat shape yields `DuplicateFinish`. All mutations reverted; `git diff --stat -- crates/` verified empty.
- **Eleven fakes**, each a single-rule perturbation of the *same* scenario's conforming sequence, so none can be rejected for the wrong reason.
- **Thirteen `#[should_panic]` harness tests** covering every way a scenario could go quietly useless: no gate, a gate that withheld nothing, an empty stream, a wrong tool name, a wrong or absent `FinishReason` declaration, a lying `encodes_stop_reason`, an unpinned decline, a stale pinned decline, a drifted decline reason.
- **Positive-evidence floors** run before the assertions, and every scenario runs under a timeout — a stream that never ends fails rather than hanging.

## Design notes worth knowing

**Assertions are made at the `Model::invoke` boundary, not against translators.** The contract is stated on `invoke`, and one of the two historical defects was a *driver* bug — the translator buffered the stop reason correctly; the driver never flushed it. A translator-only harness would have gone green against it.

**`encodes_stop_reason` measures the bytes about to be served**, rather than restating the harness's own expectation. That is the only thing that can distinguish `ErrorAfterStopReason` from `ErrorMidGeneration`, whose observable events are identical.

**Fixtures are transcribed from captured traffic, never invented.** Two shapes had no capture in the repo and were reported BLOCKED rather than derived from unit tests; both were captured live on 2026-08-20 and transcribed. The Gemini capture then contradicted the plan's own instruction about `usageMetadata` placement — fidelity won, which cost a non-vacuous floor and is documented at the site.

**Declines are pinned in both directions.** `DECLINED` fails on an unexpected decline *and* on an expected decline that stopped happening, so a red assertion cannot be quietly converted into a skip. Eight rows, all structural — e.g. `openai/responses` cannot express three scenarios because its terminal event builds `Usage` and `Finish` together.

## Contract wording

Doc-only, at four `-core` sites (`Model::invoke`, and `ToolCallDelta` on both the variant and the field in `model.rs`, plus `agent.rs`), the book's provider page, and two Bedrock comments that asserted `Usage` must precede `Finish` — the misreading that made emitting `Finish` inline look correct in the first place.

No `version` field is edited anywhere; release-plz performs the `-core` bump itself. Note the dependent cascade reaches **every** dependent of `-core`, so the release PR will touch most of the workspace.

## Verification

All six CI gates pass locally at head: `fmt`; `clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace --all-features` (170/170 blocks, 0 failed); `cargo doc` with `RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings`; doc coverage 100.0% (1375/1375) on the pinned nightly; `mdbook build`.

- [`MockModel` ignores its cancellation token](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-563) — violates the clause this PR tightens
- [Unify the `finish()` return shape](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-564) — four shapes, not the three the ticket listed; now guarded by this suite
